opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a really instructive example. The early approach, and I think this was true of Waymo and of most of the self-driving efforts at the time, was essentially to write down rules for what the car should do in each situation. If you're approaching a four-way stop and another car arrived first, you wait. If there's a pedestrian at the crosswalk, you stop. And so on. That sounds reasonable, but what you find is that the world keeps producing situations the rules didn't anticipate, and then the rules start to conflict with each other or simply don't apply.

The famous example was the four-way stop. The rule says you wait until the other cars have gone. But human drivers don't actually behave that way. They creep forward, they negotiate, they signal intent with the motion of the car. So the Waymo car would sit there, politely waiting, and it would never get to go, because the humans were all inching forward and the rule said "someone else is moving, so I wait." The car was frozen by its own rules.

What that reveals, I think, is that rules are really a compressed summary of the consequences of actions. The reason we have a rule like "wait your turn at a four-way stop" is that it usually leads to good outcomes: nobody crashes, everyone gets through reasonably efficiently. But the rule isn't the thing we actually care about. What we care about is the outcomes: safety, getting where you're going, not annoying other people unnecessarily. When you hard-code the rule and throw away the reasoning behind it, you lose the ability to handle cases where following the rule no longer achieves the purpose it was designed for.

So the right way for an AI system to choose actions, and this is really the classical view of rational agency we've had in AI for a long time, is to think about what will happen if I do this versus that, and which of those outcomes is better according to the objectives. At the four-way stop, a car that reasons about consequences can recognize that if it creeps forward a little, the other drivers will see it and let it go, and that's safe. It can treat the other drivers as agents with their own intentions, predict how they'll respond, and act accordingly. That's a kind of lookahead, a planning process, rather than a lookup table.

And of course this connects to the bigger issue I've been worried about for years, which is where the objectives come from. Once you move from rules to reasoning about consequences, everything depends on the system having the right idea of what's good and bad. If you specify the objective wrongly, a system that is very good at pursuing objectives will pursue the wrong thing very effectively. In driving the objectives are relatively well understood, but even there you have tradeoffs between safety, speed, comfort, and courtesy that are hard to write down precisely. That's why I argue that systems should be uncertain about the objective and should learn about human preferences from human behavior, rather than having a fixed objective plugged in.

So the lesson from early self-driving cars is a kind of microcosm. Rigid rules break. Reasoning about consequences works much better. But reasoning about consequences is only as good as your understanding of what humans actually want, and getting that right is, I think, the central problem of AI.

r001.rationale: It says the world produces situations the rules did not anticipate, and that the rules may conflict or not apply.

r002.rationale: It proposes comparing what will happen under different actions, predicting how other drivers will respond, and using lookahead planning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the interesting thing about that early system is that it was, in a sense, a very old-fashioned kind of AI. You had engineers trying to anticipate every situation the car might find itself in and writing down what to do: if there's a pedestrian here, slow down; if the light is yellow and you're this far from the intersection, stop; and so on. And the trouble is that the world is enormously richer than any list of rules you can write down. So the car would encounter a situation the engineers hadn't thought of, perhaps a cyclist doing a track stand at an intersection, rocking back and forth, and the rules would say, well, the cyclist is moving, so wait. And it would wait forever. Or a plastic bag blowing across the road, and the car can't tell whether it's a bag or a child.

What that reveals, I think, is something fairly fundamental about how we ought to think about decision making in AI. The rules are really a kind of compiled approximation of what you actually want, which is a safe, efficient, courteous journey from A to B. The engineers had the objective in their heads, and they were trying to translate it into behavior one case at a time. But the translation is lossy. Every rule you write is a guess about what the right action is under circumstances you've imagined, and it says nothing at all about circumstances you haven't.

The alternative, which is really the whole project of decision theory going back to the eighteenth century, is that the system should be choosing actions according to their expected consequences, given what it knows and doesn't know, and given what the human actually cares about. So instead of "if cyclist is moving, wait," you have a system that understands that the point of waiting is to avoid a collision, that reasons about the probability that this particular cyclist is about to enter the intersection, and that weighs the small risk against the cost of sitting there blocking traffic. That kind of system can handle the situation it's never seen, because it isn't matching situations to prescriptions; it's reasoning from goals.

Now, the important caveat, and this is the part I care about most, is that the objective itself is also something the engineers only partly understand. We don't actually know how to write down in full what "a good journey" means, any more than we know how to write down the rules. So the lesson isn't just "replace rules with an objective function." It's that the system has to be uncertain about what the objective is, and it has to behave sensibly under that uncertainty. If the car is unsure whether the human would rather be late or rather risk a slightly aggressive merge, it should err on the side of caution, it should be willing to be corrected, it should perhaps ask. A rule-based system can't do that, because it has no representation of what it doesn't know. And a system with a fixed, confidently specified objective can't do it either, which is in some ways worse, because it will pursue a slightly wrong goal with great competence.

So I'd say the early Waymo experience is a nice small-scale illustration of the general point. Brittleness comes from treating the designer's knowledge as complete, whether that knowledge is expressed as rules or as a single reward signal. Robustness comes from building systems that reason about consequences and that treat human preferences as something to be learned and deferred to, rather than something already known.

r001.rationale: It says the world is richer than any list of rules and gives examples of situations the engineers had not anticipated.

r002.rationale: It advocates reasoning about expected consequences, but does not clearly describe comparing projected sequences of actions and the world’s responses.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think they reveal the limitations of trying to specify intelligent behavior as a collection of rules. You can say, “Stay in your lane,” or “Don’t cross a double yellow line,” but then you encounter a delivery truck blocking the road, and following the rule literally means sitting there forever. Adding exceptions gets you only so far, because the world keeps producing situations you didn’t anticipate.

The more general approach is to choose actions by considering their possible consequences: what might happen if I do this, how likely is it, and how desirable is that outcome? In driving, you’re balancing making progress with safety and the effects on other road users, under considerable uncertainty about what they’ll do.

And that raises a further question: how does the system know which outcomes are desirable? We shouldn’t assume that we can write down a perfectly complete objective any more than we can write down a perfectly complete set of driving rules. The system needs to recognize uncertainty about what people want, as well as uncertainty about the world.

r001.rationale: It says rule-based systems encounter situations they did not anticipate and that adding exceptions cannot cover the continually varied world.

r002.rationale: It proposes weighing possible consequences, their likelihood, and desirability, but does not describe comparing projected sequences of actions and the world's responses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they reveal the limitations of trying to specify intelligent behavior as a collection of rules. You can say, “Don’t cross the double yellow line,” but then a delivery truck stops in front of you, and following that rule literally means sitting there forever. Adding exceptions becomes an endless process, because the world keeps presenting combinations you didn’t anticipate.

What you really want is a system that considers the possible consequences of its actions and chooses among them according to how desirable those consequences are. Traffic rules matter enormously, but they operate within a broader purpose: getting people where they need to go safely, while taking account of everyone else on the road. And because the system can’t know exactly what will happen, it has to reason about uncertainty as well. That’s the distinction between prescribing behavior and giving a system a basis for choosing behavior.

r001.rationale: It says rule exceptions become endless because the world presents combinations the system did not anticipate, so fixed rules cannot cover every circumstance.

r002.rationale: It proposes choosing based on possible consequences, but does not describe comparing projected sequences of actions and the world's responses.
